claims.text: Controlled low-temperature annealing of a eutectic high-entropy alloy will trigger an FCC-to-HCP transformation.
The annealing-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation is a dynamic TRIP process.
FCC-to-HCP transformation refines the microstructure.
Low-temperature annealing will simultaneously increase strength and ductility.
The starting eutectic HEA has an as-cast dual-phase FCC+B2 microstructure.
The starting alloy has relatively coarse lamellae.
The annealing treatment should be conducted under inert gas or vacuum.
An annealing window exists that activates FCC-to-HCP transformation without full recrystallization or undesirable coarsening.
Fine HCP transformation products will nucleate and propagate within the original FCC matrix.
Formation of HCP products will increase the density of interphase boundaries.
Metastable FCC can transform to HCP through the glide of partial dislocations during plastic deformation.
The transformed microstructure increases dislocation accumulation at phase interfaces.
Progressive FCC-to-HCP transformation during deformation produces a steady hardening effect with increasing strain.
The TRIP effect can promote both strength and plasticity.
Annealed samples will have higher yield strength than untreated as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will have greater strain-to-failure than untreated as-cast samples.
Precipitation strengthening contributes to the predicted strength increase.
The beneficial response requires a sufficient fraction of metastable FCC phase.
An overly stable FCC phase will prevent the required TRIP response.
Poorly selected annealing temperature or duration can cause detrimental coarsening or unwanted phase transformations.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes FCC-to-HCP transformation to the annealing treatment, whereas the mechanism describes it as slip-induced dynamic TRIP occurring during plastic deformation. It is therefore unclear whether HCP forms during annealing or only during subsequent mechanical testing.

The HCP phase is alternately described as precipitates producing precipitation strengthening and as a displacive FCC-to-HCP transformation product. These are distinct mechanisms, and no precipitation reaction is specified or supported.
